amendments.rule: An English function word the ASV supplies for an adverbial accusative belongs to the noun whose case-function licenses it — *as a bird*, *to your mountain* — and is never `added`. **An appositional or measure nominal the ASV introduces with a supplied preposition is read the same way.** Where a noun or numeral stands in the clause with no preposition and no object marker on it, and the ASV writes an *of* or a *for* before it to state what that nominal contributes, the word is that nominal's own rendering: `אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` → *the length ... of five and twenty thousand*, `תֹּכֶן אֶחָד` → *of one measure*, `לַאֲחֻזָּה עֶשְׂרִים לְשָׁכֹת` → *for a possession ..., for twenty chambers*, `חַטָּאת שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *a he goat ... for a sin offering*. It goes to the word it stands before, which is the noun or numeral opening that phrase, and the unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31; the supplied preposition is never the head. **Read *an *of* or a *for** as any preposition the ASV writes for the nominal's own contribution, and not as a closed list.** What licenses the word is that a bare nominal stands in the clause and the English needs a word to say what it contributes there, so read the condition and not the lemma, exactly as rule 40 does for the preposition it silences: a comparative *as* before a nominal the ASV construes as a comparison — `פַּלְגֵי מַיִם` → ***as*** *the watercourses* — an agent *by* before a bare nominal the ASV construes with a passive participle — `מְבַקְשֵׁי מָוֶת` → *driven to and fro* ***by*** *them that seek death* — and a *with* or an *in* before a nominal standing in a `מִן` comparison — `אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים` → ***with*** *a contentious woman*, `בֵּית חָבֶר` → ***in*** *a wide house* — all go to the nominal on the same terms as an *of* or a *for*, and this rule's first sentence already writes *as* and *to* for the adverbial accusative. Three limits, each stated where it belongs. A word an object marker stands to take is the marker's under rule 16, and an *as for* the ASV writes before a topicalized phrase no marker and no preposition stands on is `added` under that rule rather than this one, since a nominal's fronting is not a case-function. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own bare object is the verb's under rule 44, and this rule's own closing paragraph disposes of one a predicate's valency needs. And a coordinating or subordinating connective the ASV writes beside such a phrase is not a word spent on the nominal at all: rules 14 and 55 count those against the morphemes that could carry them. **A preposition standing elsewhere in the clause that has already taken an English word of its own does not make such a word a surplus.** Rule 52's count governs two English words offered to one morpheme, and here each phrase has a rendering of its own, so a written `לְ` rendered *for a possession* does not silence the *for* the ASV writes before the phrase standing beside it. **But an English preposition the ASV writes again over a member the Hebrew coordinates under one written preposition is that preposition's, and not the bare nominal's.** Hebrew gaps a preposition in the later members of a coordination where English rewrites it, and the word the ASV writes there is the distributed scope of the one written morpheme: it joins that morpheme's possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, however much stands between and whatever word the ASV chose for the members in between. `בְּכֹל מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה וַאֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לְפָנָיו` → *among all the kings of Judah, nor* ***among*** *them that were before him* gives the second *among* to the one `בְּ`, and `בַּחְלַח וּבְחָבוֹר נְהַר גּוֹזָן וְעָרֵי מָדָי` → *in Halah and on the Habor the river of Gozan and* ***in*** *the cities of the Medes* gives the third preposition to the first `בְּ`, across the second member's own `בְּ` holding the *on* written for it. What tells this from the preceding sentences is order and repetition together, not that the nominal is bare: this sentence governs a member coordinated after a written preposition of its own phrase whose English the ASV has simply written again, and the earlier sentences govern a nominal standing before any such preposition, or in a phrase where none is written at all. So read whether a preposition of that phrase stands earlier in the coordination before giving the word to the noun — `הַנִּמְצָא בֵית־יְהוָה וּבְאֹצְרוֹת בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ` → *that was found* ***in*** *the house of Jehovah, and in the treasures of the king's house* leaves its first *in* to `בַּיִת` under this rule's first sentence, because the written `בְּ` stands after it and nothing is being repeated. Test by subtraction as elsewhere: ask whether the English word states what a bare nominal contributes to its clause, or restates a relation a written preposition already carries over that member. **But the noun must be present.** Where the ASV supplies the head noun as well as the function word, no morpheme is there to carry either, and the whole supplied phrase is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת בַּחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת` → *five hundred* ***in length*** *by five hundred* ***in breadth*** supplies both the preposition and the dimension noun in a clause whose Hebrew names neither, exactly as the italic ***reeds*** of `חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` supplies a measure noun. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English and ask whether a Hebrew noun standing in the clause has lost the relation it bears, or whether what has gone is a noun the Hebrew never wrote. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter. **But run the direct-object question before that test, because the test cannot answer it.** Where the bare noun is the direct object of a verb standing in the clause, rule 44's supplied-preposition clause governs and the word joins that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, whatever preposition the ASV chose and whether or not another would have served. A recasting that makes a transitive Hebrew verb intransitive in English always leaves the translator a relation to choose, so the availability of another word says nothing about which morpheme licenses the one written, and only what governs the noun in the Hebrew can tell the two apart. `וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח` → *he will increase* ***in*** *learning* and `מְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם` → *go right* ***on*** *their ways* both give the word to the verb, because `לֶקַח` and `אֹרַח` are what those verbs govern, and rule 44's own examples — *have done violence to my law*, *hast greedily gained of thy neighbors* — are the same construction written without the recasting. What the preceding sentence governs is a complement no verb takes as its object: the accusative of manner of `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר`, the accusative of specification of `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ`, and the `מָלֵא` case, where an adjective and not a verb is the predicate. Read MACULA's clause for what governs the noun, as this rule's third limit already directs in deferring to rule 44, and where no verb governs it the preceding sentences stand as before. **But that deferral reaches a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as an English verb, and no other.** Rule 44's clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, so it presupposes an English verb doing the reaching. Where instead the ASV dissolves the governing verb into the noun's own English phrase — writing it as an attributive adjective, as a participle, or as any word that takes no object of its own — no English verb reaches that noun at all, rule 44's clause has nothing to govern, and the preceding sentences stand: the supplied preposition states what the whole recast phrase contributes to the clause the ASV has left standing, and it belongs to the noun. `הֵעֵזָה פָנֶיהָ וַתֹּאמַר לוֹ` → *And* ***with*** *an impudent face she said unto him* gives *with an face* to `פָּנֶה`, the indefinite article the noun's own under rule 15, and leaves `עָזַז` the bare *impudent*, though `פָּנֶה` is what that verb governs in the Hebrew. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English preposition and ask whether an English verb has lost the reach to its object, or whether a phrase standing beside the clause's own verb has lost the relation it bears to it. Read what the ASV made of the verb before running the direct-object question, since a recasting that keeps the verb a verb is what the preceding paragraph governs, and PRO.7.16 → *I have spread my couch* ***with*** *carpets* and PRO.7.13 → ***with*** *an impudent face* are the two shapes in one chapter.
amendments.why: PRO.7.13 met a case rule 33's direct-object paragraph had not considered. `הֵעֵזָה פָנֶיהָ` writes `פָּנֶה` as the direct object of `הֵעֵזָה`, so that paragraph as it stood sent the supplied *with* to the verb under rule 44 — but the ASV recast `הֵעֵזָה` as the attributive *impudent* inside the noun's own phrase, so there is no English verb for the preposition to reach an object through, and rule 44's clause is written in terms of exactly that reach. The chapter shows both shapes: PRO.7.16 and PRO.7.17 keep the verb a verb and give the supplied *with* to it, while PRO.7.13 does not. The qualification is added where the over-broad sentence stands rather than returned as a new rule pointing back at it, and it changes nothing the corpus already settles: rule 44's cited examples all keep the Hebrew verb as an English verb.

conventions: Head of a modifier-plus-generic rendering. Where a Hebrew substantive is rendered by an English modifier and a generic noun, this chapter heads on the modifier, by rule 31's subtraction: `פְּתָאיִם` → *the simple ones* on *simple*, `רְחֹבוֹת` → *broad places* on *broad*, `שְׁלָמִים` → *peace offerings* on *peace*, `חֲטֻבוֹת` → *striped cloths* on *striped*, `עֲצֻמִים` → *a mighty host* on *mighty*, `כֶּסֶא` → *full moon* on *full*. The one unit headed on the noun is `נַעַר` → *A young man* at PRO.7.7, where rule 31's class-noun tie-break is met: the ASV writes a bare *the man* for `אִישׁ` at PRO.7.19, so *young* is the specifier distinguishing one class word from another. Read the chapter for that usage before moving a head onto the English noun; where no same-class word is written alone, the modifier heads.

An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter. **But run the direct-object question before that test, because the test cannot answer it.** Where the bare noun is the direct object of a verb standing in the clause, rule 44's supplied-preposition clause governs and the word joins that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, whatever preposition the ASV chose and whether or not another would have served. A recasting that makes a transitive Hebrew verb intransitive in English always leaves the translator a relation to choose, so the availability of another word says nothing about which morpheme licenses the one written, and only what governs the noun in the Hebrew can tell the two apart. `וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח` → *he will increase* ***in*** *learning* and `מְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם` → *go right* ***on*** *their ways* both give the word to the verb, because `לֶקַח` and `אֹרַח` are what those verbs govern, and rule 44's own examples — *have done violence to my law*, *hast greedily gained of thy neighbors* — are the same construction written without the recasting. What the preceding sentence governs is a complement no verb takes as its object: the accusative of manner of `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר`, the accusative of specification of `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ`, and the `מָלֵא` case, where an adjective and not a verb is the predicate. Read MACULA's clause for what governs the noun, as this rule's third limit already directs in deferring to rule 44, and where no verb governs it the preceding sentences stand as before. **But that deferral reaches a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as an English verb, and no other.** Rule 44's clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, so it presupposes an English verb doing the reaching. Where instead the ASV dissolves the governing verb into the noun's own English phrase — writing it as an attributive adjective, as a participle, or as any word that takes no object of its own — no English verb reaches that noun at all, rule 44's clause has nothing to govern, and the preceding sentences stand: the supplied preposition states what the whole recast phrase contributes to the clause the ASV has left standing, and it belongs to the noun. `הֵעֵזָה פָנֶיהָ וַתֹּאמַר לוֹ` → *And* ***with*** *an impudent face she said unto him* gives *with an face* to `פָּנֶה`, the indefinite article the noun's own under rule 15, and leaves `עָזַז` the bare *impudent*, though `פָּנֶה` is what that verb governs in the Hebrew. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English preposition and ask whether an English verb has lost the reach to its object, or whether a phrase standing beside the clause's own verb has lost the relation it bears to it. Read what the ASV made of the verb before running the direct-object question, since a recasting that keeps the verb a verb is what the preceding paragraph governs, and PRO.7.16 → *I have spread my couch* ***with*** *carpets* and PRO.7.13 → ***with*** *an impudent face* are the two shapes in one chapter.
amended.why: PRO.7.13 met a case rule 33's direct-object paragraph had not considered. `הֵעֵזָה פָנֶיהָ` writes `פָּנֶה` as the direct object of `הֵעֵזָה`, so that paragraph as it stood sent the supplied *with* to the verb under rule 44 — but the ASV recast `הֵעֵזָה` as the attributive *impudent* inside the noun's own phrase, so there is no English verb for the preposition to reach an object through, and rule 44's clause is written in terms of exactly that reach. The chapter shows both shapes: PRO.7.16 and PRO.7.17 keep the verb a verb and give the supplied *with* to it, while PRO.7.13 does not. The qualification is added where the over-broad sentence stands rather than returned as a new rule pointing back at it, and it changes nothing the corpus already settles: rule 44's cited examples all keep the Hebrew verb as an English verb.

report: Read all 24 candidate lemma groups end to end, plus the full dump for the `added` units the table is blind to. Twenty-three groups are the ASV rendering one word differently where the source or the ASV's own printed wording licenses it, not splits.

Prepositions: `בְּ` splits from its construct noun wherever the ASV writes a word for each (7.6 *at the window*, 7.9 *In the middle*, 7.19 *at home*, 7.21 *With the flattering*) and fuses under rule 30 wherever one English word carries the pair with nothing written for the noun's own lexeme (7.20 `בְּיָדוֹ` → *with*, `לְיוֹם` → *at*). That is rule 30's one-rendering test applied uniformly, not two analyses.

`לְ` before an infinitive: *That* at 7.5 (rule 52), *to* twice at 7.15, `unrepresented` at 7.10 where the ASV writes *there met him* with no preposition (rule 40). Same construction, different ASV wording. `לְ` at 7.4 divides the same way — *unto wisdom* written, *call understanding* bare.

Articles: every `הַ` takes a written *the* where the ASV writes one before its own word and is `unrepresented` where the ASV writes none for the phrase at all (7.4 twice, 7.20 `הַכֶּסֶף`). Construct nouns take a supplied *the* only where no article morpheme stands in the chain, and the chapter counts the ASV's *the*s the same way in all eleven chains.

One real inconsistency, patched: PRO.7.20 headed `כֶּסֶא` → *full moon* on *moon*, while the chapter's five other modifier-plus-generic substantives all head on the modifier. Rule 31's subtraction (*moon* alone is any moon, as *place* alone is any place) and its class-noun tie-break (no bare *moon* written for a same-class word here) both point at *full*. Head moved; no edge changed. `נַעַר` → *A young man* at 7.7 stays on *man*, because the tie-break is met there — the ASV writes a bare *the man* for `אִישׁ` at 7.19 — and that difference is now recorded as a convention.

BSB: none of the seven disagreements is an error. Five are rule 40 recastings that leave a preposition no English word (7.4, 7.10, 7.13 twice, 7.19); two are suffixes and one article the ASV writes nothing for (7.13, 7.19, 7.20 twice), and one is the paragogic he of `לְכָה` at 7.18, which rule 32 marks `unrepresented` and which the rule itself names as the standing BSB convention difference. No accepted edge was changed for the aggregate.

Checked and let stand: PRO.7.13 gives the supplied *with* of *with an impudent face* to `פָּנֶה` under rule 33 rather than to `הֵעֵזָה` under rule 44, even though `פָּנֶה` is that verb's object in the Hebrew, because the ASV has recast the verb as the attributive *impudent* and no English verb reaches the noun. Rule 33's direct-object paragraph did not consider that shape, so the reading is returned as an amendment to rule 33 rather than left as a chapter-local judgment.

The six repeated verse notes the validation report flags (supplied *the* on a construct, *of* on the rectum, indefinite article on the noun, possessive on the suffix, supplied determiner on the noun) are verbatim restatements of rules 15, 18, 19 and 29 and are deliberately not logged as conventions.
